lens: Could a competent Caltrans employee with zero ERIS training do their job on day one? I judged orientation (do I know where I am and where to start), wayfinding (can I get to the thing I need without knowing the data model), vocabulary (is every word one a maintenance or GeoTech employee already uses), next-step clarity (does the screen tell me what to press and what happens after), error prevention (can I commit something irreversible by accident or lose work), consistency (does the same fact look the same everywhere), and how much a screen asks a newcomer to hold in their head. Learnability was weighted most heavily but every criterion was scored. I judged the four directions as written against brief-core.md's live measurements, first-day walkthroughs and vocabulary table, brief-screens.md's per-screen data verdicts and brief-research.md, and I checked the current code (web/src/ui/AppShell.tsx useNavSections, web/src/App.tsx route table, web/src/api/assessments.ts, web/src/api/types.ts) where a proposal's feasibility depended on it.

criteria.name: implementation cost and fit with the current codebase

perCriterion.reason: It is the only direction that removes the newcomer's prerequisite rather than relabelling it: the Incident becomes the only object anyone navigates to, Assessment/Submission/Event Group become tabs of it, navigation drops to Home / Incidents / Map, and the same four facts (status, holder, next step, your move) appear in the same order on every card, banner and Home row.

Each tab is defined by the decision made there ('this tab is about people', 'forms live in the Form tab'), lists are capped at five facts per card, one Incidents list replaces four record pages, and the rule that form-level status never renders outside the Form tab collapses three competing status vocabularies into one.

Four designed compositions (bottom bar / 64px rail / 240px sidebar, drill-in below 840, two-pane above), content starting at 56-104px instead of 700px, card lists below 840, one map per screen, 3D only on request, and terrain drawing honestly declared unavailable on phones; the only soft spot is a seven-tab strip that scrolls horizontally on a phone.

perCriterion.criterion: implementation cost and fit with the current codebase
perCriterion.reason: 56 days over four phases, the case file lives at the existing /incidents/:id route, new @theme breakpoint tokens are added alongside legacy sm/md/lg/xl and removed page by page, and the reuse list is accurate (assessmentModel, ModalDialog, submissionDetailModel, WorkflowTree label maps, MissionCenter MapView) — but a redirect table for every legacy URL is load-bearing and the case loader fires 6-8 parallel calls until the /case endpoint exists.

Objects and the state machine are untouched and the subtle rules are right: office-scoped finalize, reviewer authority by assignment with CONSULTED marked informational, multiple technical forms per assessment kept behind a form selector, Finalize explicitly distinguished from Mark resolved, duplicates linked rather than deleted, and structured requested_fields for the reporter loop.

24/44px targets, 14px body and 12px caption floors, reflow at 320px, no nested scroll, no hover-only affordances, aria-current='step' on the rail and an explicit instruction that the ActionSheet must wrap the existing ModalDialog rather than reimplement focus management; it does not address the per-theme brand/good/bad text contrast failure that spec-language flags.

strengths: The one structural move that actually answers brief-core's deepest finding — 'a newcomer has to learn the data model before they can do their job' — by making the Incident the only navigable object and every other backend object a tab inside it.
Three destinations mapped to the three questions people actually ask (what needs me / look something up / where is it), the smallest nav of the four and identical on every device.

One card grammar (title, location line, status + holder, age, one primary action) reused by Home, Incidents, Map list, Event page and preview panes — consistency is the cheapest learnability multiplier and this proposal buys the most of it.

The nine-step progress rail from Reported to Resolved with dates and names, terminal dispositions rendered as their own end states, answers 'where is it and who has it' on one screen; the brief lists that as the top mental-model gap for four of seven personas.

Receipts everywhere: toast plus timeline entry plus a 'Recently done' row, so nothing an item does after you act on it is invisible — this fixes both coordinator confusions (triaged reports vanish; sent-back reports look new).

Role-aware Home with focus-ordered sections and an admin default of 'Assigned to me' plus a System health strip that surfaces the silent failure modes (district with no coordinator, review with no reviewer, package not generated).
Cross sections save to the incident instead of an invented 'Project', removing one of the two objects the brief rates 'High' confusion.
fatalFlaws: Seven tabs per incident (Overview, Report, Assessment, Form, Evidence, Site, History) are a new recall task: a first-day user must guess whether 'who has it' is on Overview or Assessment, and whether the engineer's questionnaire is under Form or Report; on a phone the strip scrolls horizontally so not all seven are even visible at once.

Event Group loses its destination and becomes a filter of Incidents plus a light page reached from a case file — yet it is the object brief-core rates highest for confusion and it is the first decision a coordinator is asked to make; a chief looking at a multi-incident storm has no browsable list of events, only a 'Group by Event Group' toggle.

Until GET /incidents/{id}/case exists, opening a case file fires 6-8 parallel requests; on an iPad in the field that is the slowest first tap of the four proposals (the plan concedes this and mitigates with lazy tabs).

The legacy redirect table (/assessments/:id, /submissions/:id, /submissions/:id/photo-evidence, /mission-center/:gid/:iid, /event-groups) is load-bearing for email links and the mobile native bridge; one missed entry silently removes a path a role uses today.
stealThese: The four-fact grammar 'status, holder, next step, your move' in that fixed order on every card, banner and Home row — make it a lint-able rule, not a guideline.

'Form-level status never appears outside the Form tab; the incident-level status is the one users learn' — the single highest-leverage sentence in any of the four proposals for cutting the three-status-machine confusion.
The nine-step progress rail with terminal dispositions as their own end states ('Closed at intake — no assessment needed').
Receipts: toast + timeline entry + 'Recently done' row for every workflow action.
The admin System health strip (districts without a coordinator, items unassigned >2 days, submitted assessments with no reviewer, mobile package not regenerated since publish).
'Reviewer decision buttons enable only after the form has been opened once this session' as an error-prevention pattern for approve/return.
Cross sections attached to the incident rather than to a user-facing 'Project' container.
evidence: brief-core.md 'Journey of one incident' and the vocabulary table: five numbered objects (Incident, Event Group, Assessment, Submission, cross-section Project) with 'High' or 'Very high' confusion ratings for Event Group/Project, Assessment, Submission/GISA, Draft and Status-vs-Stage-vs-State.

brief-core.md branch-chief walkthrough: 'Every case is referenced by up to three ids (Incident #, Assessment #, Submission #, plus AS # / Sub # abbreviations) and no location on assessment cards, so cases cannot be identified'; mental-model gap 'Job: one incident that moves through people. Software: Incident, Assessment, Submission, each with its own id and page'.
brief-core.md coordinator walkthrough S2 'Choosing where to look': 'Four Operations entries (Mission Center, Event Groups, Incidents, Assessments) all plausibly hold the status of an incident'.

brief-core.md Incidents audit S3: 'The record view never shows the record: description, first_observed_at, current_stage, incident_key, office_code, reporter... are never rendered'; and 'WorkflowTreeModal/WorkflowTreeView and getWorkflowTree are never mounted, so no screen shows where an incident sits in the review chain'.

web/src/App.tsx: /incidents/:id already exists as a route, so the case file inherits the primary object's URL grammar; /assessments/:id, /submissions/:id, /submissions/:id/photo-evidence, /mission-center/:gid/:iid and /event-groups/:id are the five paths the redirect table must cover.
web/src/ui/AppShell.tsx useNavSections: today's five sections and seven entries (Workspace, Operations x4, GIS Tools, Administration, Account) versus the proposal's three destinations.

perCriterion.reason: Every role lands on a personal Inbox whose rows are named by place and by the verb that moves them, every object page opens with one Next-step banner and exactly one primary button, and 'no page ever tells the user to go act somewhere else' is stated as a law — this is the crispest next-step discipline of the four and it directly kills the walkthroughs' worst dead ends, but the newcomer still meets three separate object pages for one job.

Twenty-two screens each carry an explicit essential/secondary/hidden split with reasons that match spec-data's verdicts (ids muted and last, coordinates behind a copy action, 'Unclaimed only' expressed as a status value, duplicate counts and orientation banners removed); the only density risk is coordinator Inbox rows carrying five text lines plus a photo strip.

Four width classes with designed compositions per class, a screens-tall budget stated as measurable acceptance criteria (Inbox ≤1.5 screens, object page ≤3 on phone, form hub ≤2, zero sub-44px targets on coarse pointers, content within 120px of the top), maps capped at 45vh with expand, no nested scroll below 840px, and a three-region form only where the width exists.

perCriterion.criterion: implementation cost and fit with the current codebase
perCriterion.reason: 64 days is the highest of the four and Phase 0 redefines Tailwind's breakpoint tokens (sm 480, md 600, lg 840, xl 1200), which silently reinterprets every existing md:/lg:/xl: class in a codebase that just shipped a redesign, so every later phase ships on top of a scale change; the reuse map is otherwise the most precise in the set.

Backend objects and the state machine are untouched, and the hard cases are right: office-scoped finalize so no queue item can 403, reviewer scoping by active assignment with an admin 'All queues' escape hatch, 'Add reviewer' available in any state before Finalized (the branch chief's currently blocked task), and helper text stating that naming an engineer skips the branch-chief step but still notifies them.

Explicit 24/44px targets, a 12px text floor, focus-visible rings, focus-trapped and restorable sheets, live regions, no hover-only affordances and status never carried by colour alone; keyboard equivalents for maps are deferred to the Phase 5 sweep rather than designed into the map screen, and per-theme contrast tokens are not addressed.

strengths: 'One banner, one button' as a system-wide law, with the corollary that no page ever redirects the user elsewhere to act — this alone repairs the branch chief's blocked reviewer task and the 'Read-only record view: actions live in My Work' dead end that sends users to a queue that may not contain the item.

The five hand-offs become route-backed guided flows (/assessments/:id/delegate), so the same flow is a full page on a phone and a dialog on a desktop with no second implementation — the cleanest structural answer to the brief's dialog-on-phone failures.

The richest status vocabulary in the set: 19 states, each with both an actor sentence and an observer sentence ('Coordinator: Start triage...' / 'Others: Waiting on J. Smith (Reviewer) since Sep 2'), which is exactly what a newcomer needs when the item is not theirs.
Inbox sections 'Needs you now / Waiting on others / Done recently' with the outcome spelled out ('Accepted - sent to North GeoTech Office - Sep 1') fix both coordinator confusions at once.
People pickers as cards carrying role, office/branch and open-assessment workload, sorted by load — the exact decision data the branch chief needs and does not have today.
'Buttons are never disabled without a reason': Submit stays enabled and opens a completeness sheet listing what is missing, with links.
Measurable success criteria per screen rather than adjectives, which makes the plan testable after delivery.
fatalFlaws: The three-page hop survives: a first-day user still moves Incident page → Assessment page → Technical form hub for one job, so the object model is mitigated by banners and labels rather than removed; brief-core names this as the top mental-model gap for the branch chief, engineer and coordinator alike.

'Records' still exposes Incidents | Event Groups | Assessments as segments, so the four-plausible-destinations problem is compressed but not solved — the newcomer must still know which object holds their answer.

Redefining the Tailwind breakpoint scale in Phase 0 makes phased delivery unsafe: any page not yet migrated renders at a composition its classes were never written for, across the ~15 files that mount AppShell plus every feature page.
Highest cost (64 days) for a learnability gain that is largely copy, banner and flow discipline — all of which the cheaper directions can adopt without the structural spend.
stealThese: 'One Next-step banner, one primary button; no page ever tells the user to act somewhere else' as a non-negotiable law for every object page.
Route-backed guided flows as sub-routes of their object (/assessments/:id/delegate, /incidents/:id/triage) so a flow is a page on compact widths and a dialog on wide ones.
The per-audience statusLanguage table: every state gets an actor sentence and an observer sentence, so an item that is not yours still reads clearly.
People pickers with role, office/branch and open-assessment count, sorted by workload, plus the 'this skips branch-chief assignment; the branch chief is still notified' helper.
Never disable a primary action: 'Submit for review' always fires and opens a completeness sheet naming the missing sections with links.
The screens-tall and tap-target budget as an acceptance test to re-run against the measured baseline (700px content start, 11.1 screens, 120 sub-40px targets, 180 overflowing elements).
'Pre-filled — check' markers on the technical form's Report header so the first section is verification, not data entry.
evidence: brief-core.md branch-chief walkthrough: 'Add a reviewer to an assessment -> verdict blocked' because reviewer management renders only in My Work mode and the item leaves the queue the moment an engineer is assigned; and 'Clicking Assign engineer: one click commits with no confirmation and no success message; the item vanishes'.

brief-core.md office-chief walkthrough: 'The APPROVED list in My Work is statewide, not office-scoped, but the finalize endpoint rejects assessments outside my office' — the proposal scopes the finalize section so no item can fail.

brief-core.md reviewer+admin walkthrough: 'My Work for an admin is every step in the state... the first item auto-selected is a coordinator triage' — the proposal defaults admins to 'Assigned to me' with an explicit All queues chip.

brief-core.md live measurements: /my-work mainContentStartsAtPx 700 on both phone and iPad portrait; /submissions/3 screensTall 11.1, smallTapTargets 120, tinyTextNodes 74, canvas cards 520px wide in a 375px viewport.

web/src/ui/AppShell.tsx: the below-lg stacked navigation card and the raw role codes joined by ' · ' at line 157 are the two shell defects the proposal's Phase 0 removes; ~15 files mount AppShell directly, which is the blast radius of the breakpoint-token change.

perCriterion.reason: The within-page work is excellent (Next-step card with consequence, grouped queues with 'Recently handled', status chips that open a definition-plus-next-step popover, teaching empty states, no disabled buttons), but it keeps five destinations per role and both My Work and Assessments for chiefs, so the newcomer still faces the act-versus-browse duality and the three-object hop that the first-day walkthroughs failed on.

Every screen gets a disciplined essential/secondary/hidden pass, the /submissions worklist folds into Assessments and the photo-evidence page into Files, and ids, coordinates, duplicate counts and classification prose all go — but keeping more pages means the same facts still appear on more surfaces, which is where today's vocabulary drift came from.

Concrete and safe: cards below 768, priority-column tables above, drill-in below 1024, three-region form at 1280, content cap 1440, coarse-pointer 44px, density setting, safe-area insets, gesture opt-in on maps, content start 104px phone / 72px tablet, and it restates the hard constraint that .esri-view never receives position or z-index; the bottom-bar/rail switch at 768 leaves 640-767 (half-width iPad Split View) on the phone composition where a rail would fit.

perCriterion.criterion: implementation cost and fit with the current codebase
perCriterion.reason: 49 days, no route changes, no new object model, Tailwind's existing breakpoints untouched, useNavSections and its gates reused unchanged, and — the smartest cost control in the set — the GISA canvas card bodies are moved intact into section pages with DASHBOARD_DEFAULT_ORDER as the section list and the existing Save-draft call as autosave, so the highest-risk rewrite is a relocation rather than a re-authoring; every phase ships independently.

The most careful domain reading of the four: it flags the double state machine as a sync-only backend change, scopes the finalize list to the office, names the legacy-REVIEWER trap explicitly in UI copy, fixes canEdit to use isEngineer so canonical GEOTECH_ENGINEER accounts are unblocked, and is the only proposal that anticipates web autosave colliding with the mobile app's offline drafts and proposes an updated_at precondition.

Coarse-pointer 44px rules, a 12px text floor, density persistence, safe-area handling, reflow at 320px, no hover-only affordances, and a Phase 5 sweep that names three-theme chip contrast and keyboard equivalents for every map-driven task.

strengths: By far the best cost-to-benefit ratio: 49 days, zero route changes, zero backend dependencies before Phase 3, and six phases that each ship on their own, so the owner gets the phone/tablet fix and the plain-language pass long before the form rewrite lands.
Keeping Tailwind's existing md/lg/xl breakpoints is the correct call for a codebase that just shipped a design system; it is the only proposal that does not reinterpret existing utility classes.

Moving the existing GISA card bodies intact into section pages, reusing DASHBOARD_DEFAULT_ORDER and the existing Save-draft endpoint, de-risks the single largest file (1,335 lines) better than any competing plan.

Status chips as tap-to-open popovers carrying definition plus holder plus next step is the best contextual-help mechanic in the set: help arrives at the exact point of confusion, on touch, with no hover.
The largest statusLanguage table (27 entries) including submission statuses and workflow-tree nodes, and the only one that gives 'workflow node UNASSIGNED' a plain reading ('Nobody assigned yet').

It names risks the others miss: mobile-vs-web draft conflicts, the legacy REVIEWER role producing an empty reviewer queue, and label changes needing to be mirrored in email templates and the mobile app to avoid a new vocabulary split.
fatalFlaws: It does not fix the top-level wayfinding failure it acknowledges: chiefs still get My Work and Assessments as separate destinations with the same list-detail layout, one to act and one to browse — brief-core records exactly this as a first-day confusion where 'the difference is stated only in a grey banner', and coordinators still choose among My Work, Incidents, Map and Event Groups.

The three-object hop is fully preserved (Incident record → Assessment → Technical form), so a day-one user must still learn the data model to navigate; 'defining beats renaming' for Event Group is a smaller intervention than the brief's 'High' confusion rating supports.

The incident record still explicitly withholds workflow actions ('Actions stay in My Work (existing IA)'), keeping the record-page dead end that made a walkthrough task blocked — mitigated by a 'This step is yours' link, but the general pattern survives even though the assessment page unifies record and work modes.
Because the destination count is unchanged, the plan's learnability gains depend almost entirely on copy and component discipline holding across five pages rather than being enforced by structure.
stealThese: Keep Tailwind's existing breakpoints (md 768 / lg 1024 / xl 1280 / 2xl 1536) and add nothing — a hard rule for whichever backbone wins.
Relocate the GISA card bodies rather than rewriting them; reuse DASHBOARD_DEFAULT_ORDER as the section list and the existing Save-draft call as the autosave transport.
Status chips as tap-to-open popovers: definition, who holds it, what happens next.
The updated_at precondition plus a 'Newer changes exist — reload' notice for web autosave against mobile offline drafts.

Fix canEdit/canAct in SubmissionDetailPage to use roleModel plus assessmentPermissions instead of the literal FIELD_WORKER/ADMIN strings — this unblocks canonical GEOTECH_ENGINEER accounts on day one and is nearly free.
Say the legacy-REVIEWER trap out loud in UI copy so a user with only the legacy role understands why their review queue is empty.
The six-phase shippability discipline: no phase depends on a backend change, and each phase leaves the product better than it found it.
evidence: brief-core.md office-chief first-day confusions: 'My Work vs Assessments: both pages have an identical rail+detail layout and the same cards, but one is act and one is browse; the difference is stated only in a grey banner'.

brief-core.md engineer walkthrough S4: 'canEdit is true only for the literal roles FIELD_WORKER or ADMIN (SubmissionDetailPage.tsx:162). An engineer provisioned with the canonical GEOTECH_ENGINEER role sees a read-only page' — the proposal fixes exactly this.

brief-core.md engineer walkthrough: 'Assessment-level Request revision flips the assessment to REVISION_REQUESTED but leaves the submission SUBMITTED, so the form is locked' — the proposal flags the state-sync backend change with that reason and does not alter the state machine.

brief-core.md submission-detail audit S4: 'The checklist form is rendered on an absolutely positioned pixel canvas of fixed 520px-wide cards with mouse-only drag/resize' — the proposal retires the canvas while preserving the card bodies.
web/src/ui/AppShell.tsx useNavSections: the proposal keeps this function and its role gates unchanged, which is why its shell phase is 7 days against 8-9 for the others.
brief-core.md shell note: 'Tailwind v4 defaults: sm 640, md 768, lg 1024, xl 1280, 2xl 1536' — the scale the proposal deliberately leaves alone.

perCriterion.reason: It promotes the three internal objects to the primary control of the product as layer chips and turns 'what is waiting on me' into a toggleable filter rather than a place, so a first-day user must understand a three-dimensional state (layer × scope × mine) before the screen means anything — the opposite of hiding the data model, even though its panels, consequence sentences and status table are individually excellent.

Row and panel content is lean and the hidden lists are well argued, but a statewide ArcGIS map is irreducible chrome on every screen for roles whose day-one work has no geography (reviewer reading a form, admin creating an account, office chief finalizing), and on a phone the list those roles need is demoted to a 96px sheet peek beneath the map.

The best-articulated single-surface responsive model in the set — viewport-locked, exactly one scroll region at a time, container-queried panels that render correctly at 360px in a sheet, 440px docked and full width, content starting at 56px, popups replaced by selection-driven panels — but it accepts a draggable nonmodal sheet as the primary phone interaction for occasional web users and mounts a MapView on every app open.

perCriterion.criterion: implementation cost and fit with the current codebase
perCriterion.reason: Its load-bearing Phase 1 (15 days, the largest single phase) cannot ship without backend change 1: web/src/api/assessments.ts shows Assessment rows carry district and office_code but no incident title, lat/lon, county, route or post mile, so the Assessments layer cannot be plotted at all, and the stated interim of client-side filtering over existing 1000-row fetches does not produce coordinates without an N+1 join; it also deletes all five record pages and redirects every legacy route into /map, leaving no list product to fall back to.

Objects and the state machine are untouched and the edge cases are handled well — 'Submitted — needs a reviewer' as its own state, CONSULTED with no decision button, finalize consequence spelled out, duplicates linked not deleted, a routing-gap status for districts with no coordinator — though modelling an assessment as a second pin at the incident's coordinates collapses two objects onto one point, and sending a rarely-web-using field reporter into a map app to read a status is a poor fit.

The strongest explicit map accessibility of the four — every map interaction has a list equivalent, keyboard detent changes with a visible 'Expand list' equivalent, the map is inert behind a full-detent sheet, and the table view is a first-class fallback — offset by taking on the hardest surface to get right (a draggable nonmodal sheet over a live map).

strengths: One surface, one selection, one scroll, expressed as URL state (?layer=&id=) so map pin, list row and panel always agree, deep links open the right panel, and Back closes the panel instead of losing the filter — the cleanest state model of the four.

Container-queried panels: the same incident panel component is written once and works at 360px in a sheet, 440px docked and full width on a phone, which is the cheapest possible route to three device compositions.
Popup-first map selection (first tap previews with an explicit Open button) fixes the audited bug where a marker click navigates and the popup's own instruction text is dead copy.
'Waiting on me · N' appearing as the same number in the rail badge and the chip, decreasing as you act, is a genuinely good orientation anchor for a newcomer.
Route-alias search that resolves '80 / I-80 / 080 / R080' into a named suggestion ('Route 80 (I-80) in District 3 · 14 open incidents') solves the coordinator task the walkthrough rated blocked.

It is the only proposal that fully solves the map itself: no viewport reset on the 60s poll, clustering above district scale, incidents drawn directly rather than only Event Groups, and district/office scope defaults.
fatalFlaws: Layer chips named Incidents | Event Groups | Assessments make the internal object model the primary control of the whole product; the brief's evidence is that newcomers cannot tell these four destinations apart today, and renaming destinations to layers does not make them distinguishable — a coordinator must know their report is on the Incidents layer while their office's case is on the Assessments layer before anything relevant appears.

'Waiting on me' is a filter that can be switched off, not a destination. A newcomer who toggles it off, or returns via Back or a deep link with it off, sees a statewide map with no indication of what they owe; every other direction makes the queue a durable place.

The core destination is backend-blocked: Assessment rows carry no incident coordinates or title (verified in web/src/api/assessments.ts), so the Assessments layer — which is the office chief's, branch chief's, engineer's and reviewer's entire home screen — cannot be drawn until backend change 1 lands, and the proposed interim does not produce the missing geometry.

Roles whose day-one job has no geography pay a full ArcGIS MapView mount (the proposal itself estimates 1-2s plus memory pressure on older iPads) on every app open just to reach a list, and then need a second mental model (view=list) to work the way they think.
stealThese: Container-queried PanelFrame so one detail panel renders correctly as a bottom sheet, a docked panel and a full-width page without three implementations.
Popup-first map selection: first tap previews in the panel or sheet with an explicit 'Open' action; never navigate from a marker click.
'Every map interaction has a list equivalent' plus a first-class table view as the keyboard and screen-reader path — adopt this as the accessibility rule for whichever backbone wins.
The map never re-frames on a poll or a keystroke; goTo fires only on an explicit level or filter change, and 'Fit to results' is a named user action.
Route-alias search that resolves 80 / I-80 / 080 / R080 to one route and offers a counted suggestion.
URL-carried selection and filter state (?layer=&id=) so deep links from email land on the exact record with its next-step card visible and Back is never destructive.
'Recently handled by me' as the label for the post-action group — clearer than 'Done recently' about who did it.
One MapView mounted in the layout route and kept alive across panel changes rather than remounted per page.
evidence: web/src/api/assessments.ts, type Assessment: id, assessment_uuid, incident_id, submission_ids, district, office_code, state, per-step timestamps — no title, latitude, longitude, county, route or post_mile, which is why the Assessments layer cannot be plotted without backend change 1.

brief-core.md coordinator walkthrough: 'Find every open incident on I-80 in my district on the map -> verdict blocked' because the statewide map plots Event Groups not incidents, there is no district filter, and route search substring-matches ids and descriptions.

brief-core.md live measurements /mission-center: phone map top 912px and list top 1502px ('map and list never visible together on a phone'); iPad portrait map at 890px, list at 1644px; desktop 1440 is 'the only viewport where list↔map sync is usable without scrolling'.

brief-core.md Mission Center audit S3: 'Clicking/tapping a marker navigates immediately in the same click handler that ArcGIS uses to open the popup, so the popup is dead copy' and 'the map viewport is reset to the full California extent on every 60s poll and on every search keystroke'.

brief-core.md personas: the reviewer's must-see list is the technical form read-only plus attachments and workflow history, and the admin's is users, routing gaps and road-inventory release state — none of which is geographic.

brief-core.md branch-chief and office-chief walkthroughs: both roles' first-day tasks are queue tasks ('what is delegated to me', 'what must I finalize'), which map-first serves only while a filter chip happens to be on.

recommendation:
Build on case-file as the backbone. It is the only direction that removes the day-one prerequisite instead of relabelling it: Home / Incidents / Map as the whole navigation, and one role-aware case file per incident where Assessment, Technical form, Evidence, Site and History are tabs rather than destinations. Every walkthrough in brief-core fails at the same place — the newcomer must learn five numbered objects across six pages before they can act — and case-file is the only plan that makes that unnecessary while leaving Incident, Event Group, Assessment and Submission untouched in the backend.

Merge four things from task-first, which is a very close second and better on next-step discipline than the winner: (1) the law 'one Next-step banner, one primary button, and no page ever tells the user to act somewhere else', applied to the case-file Overview banner and every tab; (2) hand-offs as route-backed flows (/incidents/:id/delegate) so a flow is a full page on a phone and a dialog on a desktop from one implementation; (3) the per-audience status table where every state has both an actor sentence and an observer sentence; (4) people pickers carrying role, office and open-assessment workload sorted by load, plus 'never disable a primary action — Submit opens a completeness sheet'.

Merge three things from progressive, whose value is entirely in de-risking delivery: (1) keep Tailwind's existing md/lg/xl breakpoints and add none — explicitly reject task-first's breakpoint remap, which would reinterpret every utility class in a codebase that just shipped a redesign; (2) relocate the GISA card bodies intact into section pages using DASHBOARD_DEFAULT_ORDER and the existing Save-draft call, rather than re-authoring the 1,335-line page; (3) adopt its risk register — the updated_at precondition against mobile offline drafts, the canEdit/assessmentPermissions fix that unblocks canonical GEOTECH_ENGINEER accounts, the legacy-REVIEWER empty-queue copy, and mirroring label changes into email templates and the mobile app. Also steal its status-chip tap-to-open popover (definition, holder, next step) as the contextual-help mechanic.

Merge five things from map-first without its thesis: the container-queried panel component, popup-first map selection with an explicit Open, 'every map interaction has a list equivalent' as the accessibility rule, no map re-framing on a poll, and route-alias search (80 / I-80 / 080 / R080). Reject its layer-chip model outright — it makes the internal object model the primary control — and reject making 'waiting on me' a toggleable filter instead of a place.

Fix the winner's own three weaknesses before building: cut the case file from seven tabs to four or five by folding Report into Overview and Site into Evidence, so a phone never needs a horizontally scrolling tab strip; keep Event Groups as a browsable list (the one place I would overrule case-file and follow task-first's Records segment or progressive's destination), because the coordinator's first decision is an event decision and the object already has the brief's highest confusion rating; and treat the aggregated GET /incidents/{id}/case endpoint as a Phase 1 backend item rather than an optimisation, since a 6-8 call fan-out on an iPad in the field is the worst first tap in any of these plans.

Adopt the three specialist specs wholesale as the substrate: spec-language's vocabulary, status and role tables become one label module (no code ever renders as user text, one status per object, 'Returned for changes' never 'REJECTED'), spec-data's global rules become the density contract (place before ids, one status per row, three-tier disclosure, column budget, counts only where actionable, role-gated content not rendered at all), and spec-responsive's shell and pattern ladder becomes the layout contract. Add spec-language's accessibility checklist as the definition of done, including the per-theme --brand-text/--good-text/--bad-text contrast tokens that none of the four proposals addressed. Finally, keep task-first's screens-tall and tap-target budget as the acceptance test, re-run against the measured baseline: 700px content start, 11.1 screens on the form page, 532px canvas in a 375px viewport, 120 sub-40px targets, 180 overflowing elements.
